cards.q: What is the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity?
cards.a: A scalar has magnitude only. A vector has both magnitude and direction.

cards.q: Sort these into scalars and vectors: speed, velocity, mass, weight, distance, displacement, acceleration.
cards.a: Scalars: speed, mass, distance. Vectors: velocity, weight, displacement, acceleration.
cards.why: Weight is a force, so it has a direction. Mass does not.

cards.q: Forces of 3.0 N and 4.0 N act at right angles on an object. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force.
cards.a: 5.0 N, at 53° to the 3.0 N force.
steps: The forces are at right angles, so use Pythagoras: \(F = \sqrt{3.0^{2} + 4.0^{2}}\).
Direction: \(\tan\theta = \frac{4.0}{3.0}\), so \(\theta = 53^\circ\) from the 3.0 N force.
cards.why: A resultant is a vector: give its direction as well as its size.

cards.q: A force \(F\) acts at an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal. Write its horizontal and vertical components.
cards.a: Horizontal: \(F\cos\theta\). Vertical: \(F\sin\theta\).
cards.why: The component next to the angle takes the cosine.

cards.q: A force of 50 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. Calculate its horizontal component.
cards.a: 43 N
steps: The horizontal component is next to the angle: \(F_{x} = F\cos\theta\).
cards.why: Check that the calculator is in degrees.

cards.q: An object of weight \(mg\) rests on a slope inclined at \(\theta\) to the horizontal. Write the components of its weight along the slope and perpendicular to it.
cards.a: Along the slope: \(mg\sin\theta\). Perpendicular to the slope: \(mg\cos\theta\).
cards.why: Check with a flat surface: at \(\theta = 0\) nothing acts along the slope, and \(\sin 0 = 0\).

cards.q: A 2.0 kg block rests on a slope at 25° to the horizontal. Calculate the component of its weight acting down the slope. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\))
cards.a: 8.3 N

cards.q: Three coplanar forces act at a point and the object is in equilibrium. What must be true of the forces, and how does this show on a scale drawing?
cards.a: Their resultant is zero. Drawn to scale, tip to tail, the three forces form a closed triangle.
cards.why: Equivalently, the components in any direction add to zero.

cards.q: A student says: "An object in equilibrium must be at rest." Correct this.
cards.a: Equilibrium means the resultant force is zero. The object is either at rest or moving with constant velocity.

cards.q: Outline how to find the resultant of two forces that are not at right angles, using a scale drawing.
cards.a: Draw the forces to scale, tip to tail, and measure the line that completes the triangle.
steps: Choose a scale, for example 1 cm to 1 N.
Draw the first force as an arrow of the right length and direction.
From its tip, draw the second force at the correct angle.
The resultant is the arrow from the start of the first to the tip of the second: measure its length and its angle.

cards.q: Define the moment of a force about a point.
cards.a: The force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force. Unit: N m.

cards.q: State the principle of moments.
cards.a: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that same point.
cards.why: Both "in equilibrium" and "about a point" are needed for the marks.

cards.q: What is a couple?
cards.a: A pair of equal and opposite coplanar forces whose lines of action do not coincide. A couple produces rotation only: it has no resultant force.

cards.q: How is the moment of a couple calculated?
cards.a: One of the forces multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces.
cards.why: Not the distance from each force to the pivot: the moment of a couple is the same about any point.

cards.q: What is the centre of mass of an object, and where is it for a uniform regular solid?
cards.a: The point at which the whole mass of the object can be considered to be concentrated. For a uniform regular solid it is at the centre.

cards.q: What is the centre of gravity of an extended body?
cards.a: The point through which the whole weight of the body can be taken to act.
cards.why: It lets you replace the weight of every part of the body with a single force when taking moments.

cards.q: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and weight 100 N rests on a pivot 1.5 m from end A. Calculate the downward force needed at end A to balance it.
cards.a: 33 N
steps: The weight acts at the centre, 2.0 m from A, which is 0.5 m from the pivot.
cards.why: The weight of a uniform object acts at its midpoint.

cards.q: A uniform beam of length 6.0 m and weight 300 N rests on supports at its ends, A and B. A 600 N load sits 2.0 m from A. Calculate the upward force from support B.
cards.a: 350 N
steps: Take moments about A, so the force at A has no moment.
cards.why: Check: the force at A is 900 − 350 = 550 N, larger because the load is nearer A.

cards.q: A force acts at an angle on a spanner. A student multiplies the force by the length of the spanner to find the moment. What is wrong?
cards.a: The distance must be the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, not the distance to the point where the force is applied.
cards.why: Equivalently, use only the component of the force that is perpendicular to the spanner.

cards.q: State the two conditions for an extended body to be in equilibrium.
cards.a: The resultant force is zero, and the resultant moment about any point is zero.
cards.why: Zero resultant force alone is not enough: a couple has no resultant force but still turns the body.

cards.q: What is the difference between distance and displacement?
cards.a: Distance is the total length of the path travelled (a scalar). Displacement is the distance in a straight line from the start to the finish, in a stated direction (a vector).

cards.q: Define velocity.
cards.a: The rate of change of displacement: \(v = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}\).

cards.q: Define acceleration.
cards.a: The rate of change of velocity: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\).
cards.why: A change of direction at constant speed is still an acceleration, because velocity is a vector.

cards.q: How do you find the average velocity, and the instantaneous velocity, from a displacement–time graph?
cards.a: Average velocity: the total change in displacement divided by the time taken. Instantaneous velocity: the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that instant.

cards.q: What does the gradient of a displacement–time graph represent?
cards.a: Velocity.

cards.q: What do the gradient of a velocity–time graph, and the area under it, represent?
cards.a: The gradient is the acceleration. The area under the graph is the displacement.
cards.why: Area below the time axis counts as negative displacement.

cards.q: What does the area under an acceleration–time graph represent?
cards.a: The change in velocity.

cards.q: A ball is dropped and bounces several times. Describe its velocity–time graph, taking downwards as positive.
cards.a: A series of parallel straight lines of gradient \(g\). At each bounce the velocity changes almost instantly from positive to negative. Each bounce starts from a smaller speed than the one before.
cards.why: The lines are parallel because the acceleration is \(g\) whether the ball is rising or falling.

cards.q: Under what condition can the equations \(v = u + at\), \(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}\) and \(v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as\) be used?
cards.a: Only when the acceleration is constant (uniform), for motion in a straight line.

cards.q: You know the initial velocity, the acceleration and the displacement, and need the final velocity. The time is not given. Which equation of motion do you use?
cards.a: \(v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as\): it is the one without \(t\).
cards.why: List the five quantities s, u, v, a, t; pick the equation that leaves out the one you neither know nor want.

cards.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates at \(2.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}\) for 8.0 s. Calculate the distance it travels.
cards.a: 80 m

cards.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at \(12\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Calculate the maximum height it reaches. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), ignore air resistance)
cards.a: 7.3 m
steps: Take upwards as positive: \(u = 12\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), \(a = -9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), and \(v = 0\) at the top.
cards.why: Choose a positive direction and keep to it: here the acceleration is negative.

cards.q: A stone is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Calculate the time it takes to reach the ground. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), ignore air resistance)
cards.a: 2.0 s

cards.q: A ball is thrown straight up. A student says its acceleration is zero at the highest point. Correct this.
cards.a: Its velocity is zero at the top, but its acceleration is still \(g\) downwards throughout the flight.
cards.why: If the acceleration were zero at the top, the ball would stay there.

cards.q: Outline a free-fall method to determine \(g\).
cards.a: Time a ball falling from rest through several measured heights, and plot a graph.
marks: Release a small dense ball from rest, for example from an electromagnet.
Measure the height \(h\) fallen with a metre rule.
Measure the time of fall \(t\) electronically (light gates, or a trapdoor that stops a timer).
Repeat for a range of heights, and repeat each reading.
Plot \(h\) against \(t^{2}\): a straight line through the origin with gradient \(\frac{1}{2}g\).

cards.q: In a free-fall experiment to find \(g\), why is a small, dense ball used?
cards.a: So that air resistance is negligible compared with the weight, and the ball falls with acceleration \(g\).

cards.q: In a free-fall experiment a graph of height \(h\) against \(t^{2}\) is plotted. How is \(g\) found from it?
cards.a: \(g = 2 \times \text{gradient}\).
cards.why: \(h = \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\) matches \(y = mx\) with \(y = h\) and \(x = t^{2}\), so the gradient is \(\frac{1}{2}g\).

cards.q: Why is a hand-operated stopwatch unsuitable for timing a ball falling about 1 m?
cards.a: The fall takes about 0.45 s, and human reaction time is about 0.2 s, so the percentage uncertainty in the time would be very large.
cards.why: The uncertainty in \(t\) is doubled in \(t^{2}\), which makes it worse.

cards.q: A projectile moves freely under gravity with no air resistance. Describe its horizontal and its vertical motion.
cards.a: Horizontally: constant velocity, because no horizontal force acts. Vertically: constant acceleration \(g\) downwards. The two motions are independent.

cards.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at \(15\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) from the top of a 20 m cliff. Calculate how far from the base of the cliff it lands. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), ignore air resistance)
cards.a: 30 m
steps: Vertical motion gives the time: \(s = \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\), so \(t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 20}{9.81}} = 2.02\ \text{s}\).
Horizontal motion is at constant velocity: \(x = vt = 15 \times 2.02\).
cards.why: The initial vertical velocity is zero: the 15 m s⁻¹ is entirely horizontal.

cards.q: A ball is kicked at \(20\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) at 30° above the horizontal. Calculate the time it takes to reach its maximum height. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), ignore air resistance)
cards.a: 1.0 s
steps: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero: \(0 = u_{y} - gt\).
cards.why: Resolve the launch velocity first. Only the vertical component decides the time in the air.

cards.q: One ball is dropped and, at the same instant, another is thrown horizontally from the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which lands first?
cards.a: They land at the same time.
cards.why: Both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration. Horizontal motion does not affect the fall.

cards.q: How does air resistance change the path of a projectile, compared with the path without it?
cards.a: The projectile reaches a lower maximum height and a shorter range, and the path is no longer symmetrical: it comes down more steeply than it went up.
cards.why: Air resistance acts against the motion throughout, reducing both the horizontal and the vertical velocity.

cards.q: Explain why an object falling through air reaches a terminal speed.
cards.a: Air resistance grows with speed until it balances the weight.
marks: At first the weight is greater than the air resistance, so there is a resultant force downwards and the object accelerates.
Air resistance increases as the speed increases.
So the resultant force, and therefore the acceleration, decreases.
When air resistance equals the weight the resultant force is zero, and the object falls at a constant (terminal) speed.

edexcel.note: Edexcel uses the term terminal velocity.

cards.q: What condition is met when a vehicle reaches its maximum speed on a level road?
cards.a: The driving force equals the total resistive force, so the resultant force and the acceleration are zero.
cards.why: Resistive forces increase with speed, so the top speed depends on the engine's power and on the drag, which depends on the vehicle's shape.

cards.q: An object moves through a fluid. In which directions do the drag force and the lift force act?
cards.a: Drag acts opposite to the direction of motion through the fluid. Lift acts perpendicular to the direction of motion.

cards.q: State Newton's first law of motion.
cards.a: An object stays at rest, or continues to move with constant velocity, unless a resultant force acts on it.

cards.q: In \(F = ma\), what does \(F\) stand for, and when does the equation apply?
cards.a: \(F\) is the resultant force on the object. The equation applies when the mass is constant.
cards.why: Using a single force in place of the resultant is the most common error.

cards.q: State Newton's third law of motion.
cards.a: If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

cards.q: List the properties of a Newton's third law pair of forces.
cards.a: They are equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type, and act on different objects.
marks: Opposite in direction, along the same line.
The same type of force (both gravitational, or both contact, and so on).
They act on two different objects.
They act for the same time.

cards.q: A book rests on a table. A student says the book's weight and the normal contact force from the table are a Newton's third law pair. Why is this wrong?
cards.a: Both forces act on the same object (the book), and they are different types of force. A third law pair acts on two different objects and is the same type of force.
cards.why: The pair to the book's weight is the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth.

cards.q: A 70 kg person stands in a lift that accelerates upwards at \(1.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}\). Calculate the force the floor exerts on the person. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
cards.a: 790 N
steps: Two forces act on the person: the contact force \(R\) upwards and the weight \(mg\) downwards.
cards.why: The floor pushes harder than the person's weight (690 N): the difference provides the acceleration.

cards.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 3000 N and a total resistive force of 600 N. Calculate its acceleration.
cards.a: \(2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)

cards.q: Define gravitational field strength, and state its unit.
cards.a: The force per unit mass acting on a small mass placed in the field: \(g = \frac{F}{m}\). Unit: \(\text{N kg}^{-1}\).
cards.why: It gives the weight of a mass directly: \(W = mg\).

cards.q: What does a free-body force diagram show?
cards.a: One object only, with every force acting on that object drawn as a labelled arrow in the direction it acts.
cards.why: Forces that the object exerts on other things do not belong on it.

cards.q: Define momentum, and state its unit.
cards.a: Mass × velocity: \(p = mv\). It is a vector. Unit: \(\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

cards.q: State the principle of conservation of linear momentum.
cards.a: The total momentum of a system of objects stays constant, provided no external resultant force acts on the system.
cards.why: The condition earns a mark.

cards.q: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at \(3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision.
cards.a: \(2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

cards.q: A stationary 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at \(400\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Calculate the recoil speed of the rifle.
cards.a: \(1.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
steps: Total momentum before firing is zero, so it is zero afterwards.
\(v = -\frac{4.0}{4.0} = -1.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\): a speed of \(1.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) in the opposite direction to the bullet.
cards.why: In an explosion from rest the two momenta are equal and opposite.

cards.q: A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at \(6.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) and rebounds along the same line at \(4.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Calculate the magnitude of its change in momentum.
cards.a: \(5.0\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
steps: Take the direction towards the wall as positive: \(u = +6.0\), \(v = -4.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).
\(\Delta p = -5.0\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\), a magnitude of \(5.0\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
cards.why: Momentum is a vector. Subtracting the speeds gives 1.0, which is wrong: the velocity has reversed.

cards.q: State Newton's second law in terms of momentum.
cards.a: The resultant force on an object equals its rate of change of momentum: \(F = \frac{\Delta (mv)}{\Delta t}\).
cards.why: \(F = ma\) is the special case when the mass is constant.

cards.q: Define impulse.
cards.a: The force multiplied by the time for which it acts, equal to the change in momentum: \(F\Delta t = \Delta (mv)\).

cards.q: What does the area under a force–time graph represent?
cards.a: The impulse, which equals the change in momentum.

cards.q: Explain how a car's crumple zone reduces the force on the people inside during a collision.
cards.a: It lengthens the time over which their momentum changes.
marks: The change in momentum of a passenger is the same with or without a crumple zone.
The crumple zone increases the time taken for the car to stop.
Force is the rate of change of momentum, \(F = \frac{\Delta (mv)}{\Delta t}\).
A longer time for the same change in momentum means a smaller force.

cards.q: What is the difference between an elastic and an inelastic collision?
cards.a: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is conserved. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms. Momentum is conserved in both.

cards.q: A 2.0 kg trolley at \(3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. They stick and move off at \(2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Calculate the kinetic energy lost in the collision.
cards.a: 3.0 J, so the collision is inelastic.
cards.why: Whenever objects stick together the collision is inelastic.

cards.q: Use Newton's laws to show that momentum is conserved when two objects collide.
cards.a: The two objects have equal and opposite changes of momentum, so the total does not change.
steps: Newton's third law: during the collision the force of A on B is equal and opposite to the force of B on A.
The two forces act for the same time.
Newton's second law: force × time is the change in momentum, so the changes in momentum of A and B are equal and opposite.
The total change in momentum is therefore zero: momentum is conserved.

cards.q: Show that the newton second (N s) is equivalent to the unit of momentum, \(\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
cards.a: \(1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}\), so \(1\ \text{N s} = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2} \times \text{s} = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
cards.why: The newton in base units comes from \(F = ma\).

cards.q: Define the work done by a force.
cards.a: The force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force: \(W = Fs\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the force and the direction of motion.

cards.q: A sledge is pulled 15 m along level ground by a 40 N force acting at 60° to the horizontal. Calculate the work done by the force.
cards.a: 300 J
steps: Only the component of the force along the motion does work: \(W = Fs\cos\theta\).

cards.q: How much work is done by a force that acts at right angles to the direction of motion?
cards.a: None.
cards.why: \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\). The normal contact force on a sliding block is an example: it does no work.

cards.q: Define power, and state its unit.
cards.a: The rate of doing work, which is the rate of transfer of energy: \(P = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}\). Unit: the watt, \(1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1}\).

cards.q: Show that the power delivered by a force \(F\) moving an object at velocity \(v\) in its own direction is \(P = Fv\).
steps: Power is the rate of doing work: \(P = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}\).
Work done is force × distance: \(\Delta W = F\Delta s\).
So \(P = \frac{F\Delta s}{\Delta t} = Fv\), because \(\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}\) is the velocity.

cards.q: A car travels at a constant \(30\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) against a total resistive force of 800 N. Calculate the useful output power of its engine.
cards.a: \(2.4 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}\) (24 kW)
steps: Constant velocity means the driving force equals the resistive force: \(F = 800\ \text{N}\).

cards.q: What does the area under a force–displacement graph represent?
cards.a: The work done (energy transferred).
cards.why: This is how the work done by a force that varies is found.

cards.q: Define efficiency.
cards.a: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output power}}{\text{input power}}\), or the same ratio for energy. It can be given as a decimal or a percentage.
cards.why: It can never be greater than 1.

cards.q: A motor with an input power of 250 W lifts a 20 kg load through 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate its efficiency. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\))
cards.a: 0.59 (59%)

cards.q: State the principle of conservation of energy.
cards.a: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one form to another, so the total energy of a closed system is constant.

cards.q: The change in gravitational potential energy is given by \(\Delta E_{p} = mg\Delta h\). When is this equation valid?
cards.a: Near the Earth's surface, where the gravitational field strength \(g\) can be taken as constant over the height change.

cards.q: A roller-coaster car starts from rest and descends through a vertical height of 20 m. Ignoring friction, calculate its speed at the bottom. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
cards.a: \(20\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
steps: Gravitational potential energy lost equals kinetic energy gained: \(mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\).
cards.why: The result does not depend on the mass or on the shape of the track.

cards.q: A 60 kg skier starts from rest and descends through a vertical height of 25 m, reaching the bottom at \(18\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Calculate the work done against resistive forces. (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
cards.a: \(5.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}\)
steps: Work done against resistive forces is the difference: \(14\,700 - 9720 = 5.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}\).

cards.q: The speed of a car doubles. By what factor does its kinetic energy change?
cards.a: It becomes four times as large.
cards.why: \(E_{k} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), so kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed. With the same braking force, the braking distance is also four times as long.

cards.q: A ball rolls down a curved track and you need its speed at the bottom. Why use conservation of energy and not the equations of uniform acceleration?
cards.a: On a curved track the acceleration is not constant, so the equations of uniform acceleration do not apply. Energy conservation needs only the change in height.
